passage:
At nine, Sahil thought Vijay was the best person in the class. Vijay was tall, always grinning, and everyone wanted to sit next to him. So when Vijay said the class hamster had escaped by itself, Sahil believed it at once. When Vijay was picked as monitor, Sahil nodded. He must be clever, too. It surprised Sahil when the teacher found the cage door propped open with Vijay's ruler, and Sahil stared at the floor for the rest of the lesson.

At fifteen, Sahil watched a video by a famous cricketer-turned-influencer with brilliant reflexes and a great smile. The influencer said everyone should join a paid programme about making money. "He is so good at sport that he must know about money too," Sahil told his cousin Tanvir. Tanvir raised an eyebrow. "Being good at one thing does not make him good at all things. What has he actually done with money?" Sahil had no answer, and closed the tab to think about it.

qa.q: What did the teacher find in the hamster's cage at nine?
qa.a: The teacher found the cage door propped open with Vijay's ruler.

qa.q: How do Sahil's beliefs about Vijay and the influencer share the same pattern?
qa.a: At nine Sahil thinks tall, grinning Vijay must also be clever and honest; at fifteen he thinks the influencer with brilliant reflexes and a great smile must know about money too. One good quality spreads into a general glow until a fact or a question breaks it.

qa.q: What was Sahil probably feeling when he stared at the floor after the cage door was found?
qa.a: Sahil felt embarrassed and confused, because someone he admired had not been honest, and he had believed Vijay without question.

qa.q: What did Tanvir do that helped Sahil?
qa.a: Tanvir asked what the influencer had actually done with money, which made Sahil check the evidence instead of trusting the admiration.

grounding: The halo effect at two ages: a child who treats a tall, cheerful classmate as also smart and honest, and a teenager who trusts an admired influencer on money.

passage:
At fifteen, Afreen's friend Asif kept imitating her way of saying "tomato" in front of the group, and it drew laughs every time. Afreen put her bag down and said in a calm voice, "I don't like that, and I'd like it to stop." No laughing, no shrugging it off. Asif blinked, then said, "Got it, sorry." He changed the subject to the match on Saturday, and after that he never did the voice again.

Nine years later, Afreen was at a team lunch and joked about her colleague Kunal's habit of losing his pen. Kunal smiled thinly and looked at his plate. Afreen noticed. Afterwards she found him at the coffee machine and said, "I'm sorry, that joke was not okay. I made it about you in front of everyone. I won't do it again." She did not add that he was too sensitive. Kunal nodded and said, "Thanks. I appreciate that." The next morning he stopped by her desk and shared a biscuit.

qa.q: What did Afreen say when Asif imitated her way of saying tomato?
qa.a: Afreen said, "I don't like that, and I'd like it to stop."

qa.q: How are Afreen's stances at fifteen and twenty-four connected?
qa.a: At fifteen Afreen says stop once, calmly, and Asif changes the subject; at twenty-four she tells Kunal she is sorry, without saying he was too sensitive. First she sets a boundary, and later she repairs trust after her own joke.

qa.q: What was Kunal probably feeling when he smiled thinly at the lunch joke?
qa.a: Kunal was embarrassed and a little hurt at being teased in front of everyone, though he hid it.

qa.q: Why did Afreen's apology work?
qa.a: She named what was not okay and promised not to repeat it, without adding that Kunal was too sensitive, so the apology repaired trust instead of defending her intent.

grounding: Teasing and banter boundaries at two ages: a teenager saying stop calmly and being heard, and the same person later apologising cleanly for a hurtful joke.

passage:
At two, Jomon ran laps round the living room after lunch, shrieking with laughter, throwing cushions and refusing every suggestion. His mother Sonali glanced at the clock. It was long past his nap. Then he tripped, burst into tears and rubbed his eyes. She lifted him, dimmed the lights and said, "You are so tired, aren't you?" He was asleep in ten minutes.

At nine, Jomon slumped at his desk with his chin on his arm, yawning through the first period and snapping at a friend. His teacher did not send him out. They asked quietly after class, "You seem worn out. How is bedtime going, and how is the noise at home?" Jomon said the new baby next door cried half the night.

At twenty-five, Jomon made three small errors in a report and stopped laughing at meetings. His colleague Joseph found him alone at the kitchenette one afternoon. "You've seemed drained lately. Anything I can take off your plate?" Jomon let out a shaky breath.

qa.q: What did Sonali do after Jomon tripped and burst into tears?
qa.a: She lifted him, dimmed the lights and told him he was so tired.

qa.q: What do the three scenes show about how adults and colleagues can read tiredness in Jomon?
qa.a: At two a wild burst is a sign that a nap is overdue, at nine slumping and a short temper lead a teacher to ask about bedtime, and at twenty-five small mistakes lead Joseph to check in kindly, so each observer looks past the behaviour to the tiredness.

qa.q: How was Jomon probably feeling as he slumped at his desk at nine?
qa.a: Jomon was worn out and irritable, low on sleep because of the crying baby next door, which shortened his temper.

qa.q: What could a colleague do besides criticising the errors?
qa.a: A colleague can check in privately, as Joseph did, and ask what could be taken off the plate, since kindness helps more than gossip.

grounding: Sleep loss noticed by observers at three ages: a wild overtired toddler, a cheerful child now short-tempered in class, and a sharp colleague making small errors.

passage:
Five-year-old Pallavi crept up to her Nana Kamal as he read the newspaper with a flat, still face. "Are you angry at me?" she whispered. Kamal lowered the paper. "No, beta, I'm only thinking about the crossword. My face gets serious when I think." Pallavi let out a breath and climbed onto his lap.

At fifteen, Pallavi's friend Reena got a phone call in the corridor about her grandmother's fall. Reena's face turned rigid, eyes fixed, mouth closed. She did not cry or speak. Pallavi did not say, "Why don't you say something?" She sat beside her on the stairs, passed her water and waited. After a long time Reena said, "I can't feel anything yet."

At twenty-four, Pallavi noticed her colleague Tarun sitting with a blank expression through meeting after meeting for weeks. She did not decide that he was bored. After work she said, "You've seemed drained. Do you want me to take the client call tomorrow?" Tarun's shoulders dropped.

qa.q: What did Nana Kamal say his serious face meant?
qa.a: Kamal said he was only thinking about the crossword and that his face gets serious when he thinks.

qa.q: What do the three scenes have in common about reading a still face?
qa.a: At five a flat, still face on Kamal means only thinking; at fifteen Reena's rigid face is shock after the call about her grandmother's fall; at twenty-four Tarun's blank expression means he is drained, not bored. Pallavi answers with a question or quiet help, not judgement.

qa.q: What might Reena be feeling on the stairs after the phone call?
qa.a: Reena is probably in shock and fear about her grandmother, feeling numb, which is why her face is frozen.

qa.q: What did Pallavi do for Tarun that suited his blank face?
qa.a: She avoided judging his attitude, asked privately in kind words how he was, and offered practical help by taking the client call.

grounding: Facial stillness at three ages: a neutral face mistaken for anger, a frozen face in shock, and a blank expression from exhaustion, each read with care.

passage:
At two, Payal held out her wooden giraffe to her uncle after he handed her a picture book, then hugged his knee. Her mother whispered, "Say thank you," and Payal chirped it back, beaming at the book more than at the words.

At fifteen, she sent hearts and a row of clapping emojis under her friend Sangeeta's post about the school play, and then paused. It felt a bit easy. She typed a separate message: "The way you held the last note when your voice shook made me cry. You did that so well." Sangeeta replied in seconds: "You have no idea how much I needed that. 🙂"

At twenty-five, in a team meeting, Payal said, "Before I present the numbers, Binita found the error in our first draft last Thursday and rebuilt the whole sheet over the weekend. Without her, this would have been wrong." Binita looked up, surprised, and smiled.

qa.q: What did Payal hand over to her uncle at two?
qa.a: Payal handed her uncle her wooden giraffe.

qa.q: How does Payal's way of showing appreciation develop from two to fifteen to twenty-five?
qa.a: At two she gives a toy and a hug and repeats a prompted thank you, at fifteen she moves from quick hearts to a specific personal message, and at twenty-five she gives specific, public credit for Binita's real work in a meeting.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling when she replied that Payal had no idea how much she needed the message?
qa.a: Sangeeta was moved and grateful, feeling that the specific message meant more than a row of reactions.

qa.q: Why did Payal's credit for Binita work well?
qa.a: It was specific, timely and public, naming what Binita did and when, so Binita felt recognised and the team saw the real contribution.

grounding: Appreciation and recognition at three ages: a toddler's thank-you gestures, a teenager's shift from reactions to a specific message, and a young professional crediting a teammate in public.

passage:
At nine, Harish noticed something: every day he wore his red shirt, his cricket team won. His sister Minakshi laughed when he refused to wash it before the final. "The shirt is why we win," he said, with a straight face. She asked, "What about the day we won when you wore blue?" Harish frowned. He hadn't thought of that.

At fifteen, he saw that students who joined tuition classes scored more in the unit tests, and told his father he needed tuition. His classmate Yamini said, "The ones who go to tuition also do their homework early and have quiet study rooms. Maybe tuition isn't the only reason."

At twenty, in the college canteen, he read a headline claiming that people who drink coffee tend to live longer, and started buying a large cup every morning. Yamini looked at the article with him. "Does it say coffee causes it? Maybe healthier, richer people just drink more of it. Or people who are already ill drink less." Harish pushed the cup aside and kept reading.

qa.q: What colour was the shirt Harish thought brought his team luck?
qa.a: The shirt was red.

qa.q: What thinking mistake does Harish make at nine, fifteen and twenty?
qa.a: At nine Harish links the red shirt to wins, at fifteen tuition to higher scores and at twenty coffee to a longer life, each time deciding that one thing causes the other without asking what else might explain both.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling when Minakshi asked about the day they won in blue?
qa.a: Harish was puzzled and a little caught out, because he had not thought of that day, and he frowned.

qa.q: What could Harish ask himself the next time a headline links two things?
qa.a: He could ask whether something else, such as health or money, might explain both, or whether the link runs the other way, as Yamini suggested.

grounding: Correlation versus causation at three ages: a child's lucky shirt, a teenager crediting tuition for marks, and a student trusting a coffee headline.
